q: This type of energy is associated with motion and equals one half mass times velocity squared. A moving car has a large amount of it, and the work-energy theorem says the net work done on an object equals its change in this quantity. Raising an object converts it into potential energy. For 10 points, name this energy of motion.

This thermodynamic law states that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. It implies that heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold. For 10 points, name this law, often numbered as the second.

This 1911 discovery by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes found that mercury's resistance drops abruptly to zero below about four kelvin. Such materials expel magnetic fields in the Meissner effect. For 10 points, name this phenomenon of zero electrical resistance at low temperatures.

This type of lens is thicker in the middle than at its edges and bends parallel rays of light toward a focal point. Magnifying glasses and the lenses of eyeglasses for farsighted people use it. The human eye has one made of a flexible tissue. For 10 points, name this converging lens, whose name suggests an outward curve.

This is the term for a particle that carries the strong force between quarks, binding them into protons and neutrons. It is a massless boson that carries color charge, and its exchange is described by quantum chromodynamics. Its name suggests a sticky substance. For 10 points, name this gauge boson.

This is the lowest-energy state of a quantum harmonic oscillator, whose energy is nonzero, equal to half of Planck's constant times frequency. It is a consequence of the uncertainty principle. For 10 points, give this term, also used for the energy of the vacuum.

These are the three laws proposed by Johannes Kepler for the motion of planets, including that orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus. For 10 points, what is the general name of these laws, relating a planet's orbital period to its distance from the Sun?
This is the bending of light caused by passing through a prism, which splits white light into a spectrum. Newton studied this. For 10 points, name this separation of light by wavelength.

This is the term for the maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium position. For sound, it determines loudness, and for light, it determines brightness. The energy carried by a wave is proportional to its square. For 10 points, name this property of a wave, the height of a crest.

This physicist found that nuclear fission in uranium could produce a self-sustaining chain reaction, and directed the first nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1, in 1942. He won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics. For 10 points, name this Italian-American physicist.

In this quantum effect a particle passes through a potential barrier that it classically lacks the energy to cross. George Gamow used it to explain alpha decay, and it makes scanning probe microscopes and flash memory work. The probability falls off exponentially with barrier width. For 10 points, name this effect.

This is the term for the bending of a path of light by a massive object, predicted by general relativity and observed in the eclipse of 1919. For 10 points, name this effect, which creates Einstein rings.
Answer these questions about mechanics.
parts: What is the product of mass and velocity?
What law states that the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration?
What quantity, equal to force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot, causes rotation?

What phenomenon occurs when two waves overlap to produce a combined wave of greater or lesser amplitude?
What English scientist's double-slit experiment around 1801 demonstrated the wave nature of light?

q: In this effect, discovered by an American physicist in 1923, X-rays scattered from electrons emerge with longer wavelength than the incident beam. The wavelength shift depends on the scattering angle. It could not be explained by classical wave theory and showed that photons carry momentum. For 10 points, name this effect named for Arthur Holly.

This blue glow seen in the water surrounding nuclear reactor cores occurs when charged particles travel faster than light does in that medium. It is analogous to a sonic boom. It is named for a Soviet physicist who shared the 1958 Nobel Prize. For 10 points, name this radiation.

This boundary in the Earth separates the mantle from the outer core at a depth of about 2,900 kilometers. S waves cannot pass through the layer below it, which showed that the outer core is liquid. Beno Gutenberg discovered it in 1914. For 10 points, name this discontinuity named for the German-American seismologist.

This Milankovitch-related cycle describes changes in the shape of Earth's orbit around the Sun, varying between nearly circular and mildly elliptical over about 100,000 years. Along with axial tilt and precession, it is thought to pace ice ages. For 10 points, name this orbital parameter whose value measures how elongated an orbit is.

This Austrian-born geologist proposed that continents were once joined in the supercontinent Pangaea and drifted apart. His hypothesis lacked a mechanism and was rejected until plate tectonics. For 10 points, name this German meteorologist.

This fine-grained dark rock makes up most of the oceanic crust and builds the Hawaiian volcanoes. It is low in silica and rich in iron and magnesium. Columnar jointing in it forms the Giants Causeway in Northern Ireland. For 10 points, name this common volcanic rock.

This scale ranks minerals from one to ten based on their ability to scratch one another, with talc at one and diamond at ten. It was created by a German geologist in 1812. For 10 points, name this scale.

These large waves are generated by earthquakes under the seafloor and travel across the ocean at speeds near 800 kilometers per hour. They grow in height as they reach shallow water. For 10 points, name this kind of wave whose name is Japanese for "harbor wave."

This layer of the Earth lies between the crust and core and makes up most of the planet's volume. It convects slowly and drives plate motion. For 10 points, name this largely solid layer rich in the mineral olivine.

This is the process in which rock is broken down into smaller pieces and carried away by wind, water, and ice. Rivers carve canyons like the Grand Canyon through it. For 10 points, name this process distinct from weathering that moves sediment.

This is the point on Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake. Seismologists locate it by triangulating the arrival times of P and S waves from at least three stations. For 10 points, name this point.

This type of plate boundary occurs where two plates move toward each other, with one plate sliding under another. It creates deep ocean trenches like the Mariana Trench and volcanic arcs. For 10 points, name this process and boundary type.
This is the name for molten rock that has erupted onto the surface of the Earth. Hawaiian volcanoes produce a lot of it. For 10 points, name this material that cools to form basalt.

Sandstone, limestone, and shale are examples of this rock class, which forms when sediments are compacted and cemented together over time. Fossils are most commonly found in it, and it often shows distinct layers called strata. Unlike igneous and metamorphic rocks, it forms at or near the surface. For 10 points, name this rock class.

This scale measures the magnitude of earthquakes using the logarithm of amplitude recorded on a seismograph. A tenfold increase in amplitude corresponds to one unit. For 10 points, name this scale named for a California seismologist, now replaced by the moment magnitude scale.

This type of rock forms when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting. Marble comes from limestone and slate from shale in this process. For 10 points, name this rock class, whose name means "change of form."
This gas, making up about 78 percent of Earth's atmosphere, is the most abundant gas in it. Plants cannot use it directly, and bacteria fix it. For 10 points, name this element with symbol N.

This is the layer of the atmosphere containing the ozone layer, lying above the troposphere. Temperature rises with altitude in it because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation. For 10 points, name this layer.

This process is the transfer of water vapor to the atmosphere from plants. Together with evaporation it is called evapotranspiration. For 10 points, name the process by which plants release water vapor through leaf pores.

These deposits of unsorted sediment, from clay to boulders, are left behind by glaciers. Terminal ones mark the farthest advance of the ice, and Long Island and Cape Cod were formed from them. Lateral and medial types form along the sides and between merging glaciers. For 10 points, name these glacial deposits.

This is the term for the dense, hot, mostly iron and nickel center of the Earth. It has a solid inner part and a liquid outer part, and the motion of the liquid generates the planet's magnetic field. Its radius is a little over 3,000 kilometers. For 10 points, name this innermost layer.

This is the long ocean ridge system where new crust is created by seafloor spreading. The Mid-Atlantic one runs down the Atlantic. Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading. For 10 points, name this feature at a divergent boundary.
This relative dating principle states that in undisturbed sedimentary rock sequences, the oldest layers are at the bottom. It was proposed by Nicolas Steno. For 10 points, name this principle.

This is the name for the shaking of the ground caused by a sudden release of energy along a fault. The San Andreas fault produces many in California, and the 1906 one in San Francisco destroyed much of that city. Seismographs record them. For 10 points, name this natural disaster.
This is the term for a naturally occurring inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and crystal structure, such as quartz. For 10 points, name this basic constituent of rocks.

This climate phenomenon features the periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. It weakens trade winds and disrupts weather across the Americas. For 10 points, name this phenomenon, whose Spanish name refers to the Christ Child.

This gas, emitted when fossil fuels are burned, is the main greenhouse gas driving recent climate change. It is also absorbed by plants during photosynthesis, and dissolves in the oceans to make them more acidic. Ice cores show its concentration over hundreds of thousands of years. For 10 points, name this gas with formula CO2.
This is the water-bearing layer of permeable rock or sediment that stores groundwater and can be tapped by wells. The Ogallala is a large American example. For 10 points, name this underground layer.

In 1909 a Croatian seismologist found that seismic waves speed up abruptly at about 30 to 50 kilometers beneath continents. This marks the base of the crust and the top of the mantle. For 10 points, name this discontinuity, abbreviated to its first four letters.

This geologic era, the "age of reptiles," includes the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods. It ended with an extinction 66 million years ago. For 10 points, name this era, between the Paleozoic and Cenozoic.

This is the term for the long-term pattern of weather in a region, as opposed to day-to-day conditions. It is usually defined by averaging temperature and precipitation over thirty years or more. The Koppen system classifies types of it. For 10 points, name this average of conditions, distinct from weather.

parts: What term describes the large moving slabs that make up Earth's lithosphere?
What fault along the western coast of North America is a transform boundary?
What American geologist proposed seafloor spreading in the early 1960s?

q: This scale rates the intensity of tornadoes by the damage they cause, from zero to five. It was developed in 1971 by a University of Chicago meteorologist and revised in 2007 to account for construction quality. An EF5 has winds over 200 miles per hour. For 10 points, name this scale named for its creator.

This limit, equal to about 1.4 solar masses, is the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf supported by electron degeneracy pressure. It was calculated in 1930 by an Indian-American astrophysicist on a voyage to England. Stars above it end as neutron stars or black holes. For 10 points, name this mass limit named for a Nobel laureate.

This diagram plots stellar luminosity against surface temperature or spectral type, revealing a main sequence, giants, and white dwarfs. It was developed independently by a Dane and an American in the early twentieth century. For 10 points, name this diagram named for two astronomers, abbreviated H-R.

This law, discovered by an American astronomer in 1929, states that galaxies recede from us at speeds proportional to their distances. It provided the first evidence for the expansion of the universe. For 10 points, name this law named for an astronomer who also has a space telescope named for him.

This is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. Its radius is given by two times the gravitational constant times the mass divided by the speed of light squared. For 10 points, name this surface named for what you see happening at the horizon.
This is the closest star to Earth other than the Sun, about four light-years away. It is a red dwarf in the Alpha Centauri system. For 10 points, name this star whose name implies it is the nearest.

These pulsating radio sources were discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish. They are rapidly rotating neutron stars that emit beams of radiation. For 10 points, name these objects, whose name combines "pulsating" and "star."

This radiation, discovered by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson in 1965 as unexplained noise in a horn antenna, has a blackbody temperature of about 2.7 kelvin. It is the leftover glow from the early universe, released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. For 10 points, name this radiation, abbreviated CMB.
This planet has the largest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, and a reddish color due to iron oxide. It has two moons, Phobos and Deimos. For 10 points, name this fourth planet from the Sun.

This is the term for a star's apparent shift in position as the Earth orbits the Sun. Friedrich Bessel first measured it for 61 Cygni in 1838. For 10 points, name this effect used to measure distances to nearby stars, and the source of the parsec.

This is the name of our galaxy, a barred spiral about 100,000 light-years across containing hundreds of billions of stars. The Sun lies in the Orion Arm, roughly halfway out from the center. Its name comes from the pale band of stars visible across the night sky. For 10 points, name this galaxy.
This object, the largest planet's most famous storm, is an anticyclone that has persisted for centuries. It is large enough to engulf Earth. For 10 points, name this feature in Jupiter's atmosphere.

These are the stable points in a two-body orbital system, where a small object can remain in a fixed position relative to the two large masses. The James Webb Space Telescope orbits the second one. There are five of them in all. For 10 points, name these points named for a French-Italian mathematician.

This is the process powering the Sun, in which hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium and release energy. It requires temperatures of millions of kelvin in the core. For 10 points, name this nuclear process, whose reverse is fission.
This is the planet with the most prominent ring system, composed mostly of ice. It has a moon called Titan with a thick atmosphere. For 10 points, name this planet, the sixth from the Sun.

This is the term for a star that has exhausted hydrogen in its core and expanded, cooled, and brightened, such as Betelgeuse and Arcturus. The Sun will become one in about five billion years. For 10 points, name this stage that follows the main sequence, which can be red.

This Polish astronomer proposed in De revolutionibus orbium coelestium that the Sun, rather than Earth, is at the center of the planetary system. He published it in 1543. For 10 points, name this man.

This is the first rocky world in the solar system, closest to the Sun, with the most extreme temperature swings. A day on it lasts longer than its year in some senses. For 10 points, name this planet, smallest in the solar system.

This is the term for a large, rotating system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter held together by gravity. Edwin Hubble classified them as spiral, elliptical, and irregular. The Milky Way and Andromeda are examples. For 10 points, give this term for an island universe of billions of stars.

This is the type of supernova that results from the thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf accreting matter from a companion. Because they have consistent peak luminosity, they serve as standard candles, which showed that the expansion of the universe is accelerating. For 10 points, name this type, labeled with a Roman numeral and a letter.

This is the term for the apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere over the course of a year. The zodiac constellations lie along it, and it is inclined about 23.4 degrees to the celestial equator. Eclipses can occur only when the Moon crosses it. For 10 points, name this great circle.

This force holds planets in orbit around the Sun and keeps the Moon circling Earth. Newton explained it with a universal law in which it is proportional to the product of two masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. Einstein later described it as curvature of spacetime. For 10 points, name this fundamental force.

This astronomer used Tycho Brahe's careful observations of Mars to derive three laws of planetary motion. He found that planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus, sweep out equal areas in equal times, and obey a period-distance relation. He published them in Astronomia Nova and Harmonices Mundi. For 10 points, name this German astronomer.

This is the name of the invisible substance that makes up about 85 percent of the matter in the universe, inferred from galactic rotation curves studied by Vera Rubin. It does not emit or absorb light. For 10 points, name this substance.

This is the name for a ball of ice, dust, and rock whose gas and dust tails point away from the Sun as it nears it. The nucleus is often called a dirty snowball, and its coma forms as ices sublimate. Halley's is the most famous periodic one, returning about every 76 years. For 10 points, name this kind of small solar system body.

This dwarf planet was discovered by Clyde Tombaugh at Lowell Observatory in 1930 and was reclassified by the International Astronomical Union in 2006. It has a large moon named Charon, and New Horizons flew past it in 2015. A heart-shaped plain called Tombaugh Regio is on its surface. For 10 points, name this world.

This is the most volcanically active body in the solar system, with hundreds of volcanoes and lava lakes. Its surface is colored yellow and orange by sulfur compounds. Tidal heating from orbital resonance with Europa and Ganymede drives its activity. For 10 points, name this innermost Galilean moon.

This is the type of eclipse in which the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, casting a shadow on part of the planet. A total one reveals the faint outer corona and lasts at most about seven and a half minutes. A path of totality sweeps across the surface. For 10 points, name this eclipse, as opposed to a lunar one.

This is the dwarf planet and largest object in the asteroid belt, visited by NASA's Dawn spacecraft in 2015. It was first discovered by Giuseppe Piazzi in 1801. For 10 points, name this world named for a Roman goddess of agriculture.
This is the term for an exploding massive star at the end of its life, which can briefly outshine a galaxy. The Crab Nebula is the remnant of one seen in 1054. For 10 points, name this event.

q: These pulsating stars have a period-luminosity relation discovered by Henrietta Swan Leavitt in 1912 from observations in the Small Magellanic Cloud. Hubble used them in Andromeda to show that it lies far outside the Milky Way. They are named for a star in the constellation Cepheus, and they serve as standard candles. For 10 points, name these variable stars.

This theorem states that the integral of a holomorphic function around a closed contour in a simply connected domain is zero. A consequence is an integral formula giving the value of a function inside a contour in terms of its values on the boundary. It is a foundation of complex analysis. For 10 points, name this theorem named for a French mathematician who also names a sequence criterion for convergence.

Kurt Godel proved two theorems with this word in their names, showing that any consistent formal system capable of arithmetic contains true statements that cannot be proved within it. They ended Hilbert's program of proving consistency of mathematics. For 10 points, give the word, referring to a quality of a system being unable to prove everything true.

This formula states that e raised to i times theta equals cosine theta plus i times sine theta. A special case with theta equal to pi gives an identity linking five fundamental constants: e to the i pi plus one equals zero. For 10 points, name this formula named for a Swiss mathematician.

This is the term for a group in which the operation is commutative, named for a Norwegian mathematician who died young. The integers under addition are an example. For 10 points, give this adjective, which also names a prize in mathematics.

This is the term for the set of all vectors that a linear transformation maps to zero. Its dimension is called the nullity, and the rank-nullity theorem relates it to the rank. For 10 points, name this subspace, also called the null space.

This conjecture, one of the Millennium Prize Problems, asks whether the nontrivial zeros of a certain complex function all have real part one half. It has implications for the distribution of primes. For 10 points, name this conjecture about the zeta function.

This theorem states that if a function is continuous on a closed interval and differentiable on the open interval, there is a point where the derivative equals the average rate of change. For 10 points, name this theorem used to prove many results in calculus.

Euler solved this problem in 1735, finding that the sum of the reciprocals of the squares of the positive integers equals pi squared over six. It was posed by Pietro Mengoli and resisted attacks by the Bernoulli family. It is named for the Swiss city that was the hometown of Euler. For 10 points, name this problem.

This is the name for a number of the form a plus b i, whose conjugate is a minus b i, and whose magnitude is the square root of a squared plus b squared. For 10 points, name this extension of the real numbers.

In graph theory, this theorem says that the vertices of any planar map can be colored with at most four colors so that no adjacent regions share a color. It was first proved in 1976 by Appel and Haken using a computer. For 10 points, name this theorem about coloring maps.

This is the name of the method of finding roots of a function by iterating x minus f of x over f prime of x. It converges quadratically near simple roots. For 10 points, name this method named for an English physicist, also called the Newton-Raphson method.
This is the term for the number of ways to arrange n distinct objects in order, equal to n factorial. There are six of these of the letters A, B, and C. For 10 points, name this counting concept.

This is the type of matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros everywhere else. Multiplying any compatible matrix by it leaves the matrix unchanged, so it plays the role that the number one plays for real numbers. Its determinant is one, and it is its own inverse. For 10 points, name this matrix.

This theorem states that a continuous function from a closed ball to itself must have a point where f of x equals x. It was proved by a Dutch mathematician and implies that stirring coffee leaves some point in place. For 10 points, name this fixed-point theorem.

This is the term for the distribution with a probability density function proportional to e to the negative x squared over two, with mean zero and variance one in its standard form. The central limit theorem says sample means approach it. For 10 points, name this bell-shaped distribution.
This is the term for a statement that is assumed to be true without proof, such as the parallel postulate in Euclid. For 10 points, give this term for a starting assumption in a mathematical system.

This function, defined as the integral from zero to infinity of t to the x minus one times e to the negative t, extends the factorial to complex numbers. For 10 points, name this function symbolized by a Greek capital letter.

This is the term for a set that can be put into one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers. The integers and rationals are examples, but Cantor's diagonal argument shows the reals are not. For 10 points, name this adjective for a set the same size as the naturals.

This is the name for the theorem that states that every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one complex root. Gauss gave the first widely accepted proof. For 10 points, name this theorem of algebra.

This is the name for the series expansion of a function about zero, with coefficients given by derivatives at zero divided by factorials. The expansion of e to the x is one plus x plus x squared over two and so on. For 10 points, name this series named for a Scottish mathematician, a special case of Taylor series.

This is the term for the point where a graph crosses the vertical axis, found by setting x equal to zero. In the slope-intercept form of a line, y equals m x plus b, it is the constant b. For the parabola y equals x squared plus three, it equals three. For 10 points, name this feature of a graph.

This is the type of number that cannot be written as a ratio of two integers, such as the square root of two. The Pythagorean Hippasus is said to have proved their existence. For 10 points, name this class of real numbers.

This is the name of the constant, approximately 0.5772, defined as the limit of the harmonic sum minus the natural logarithm of n. It is named for two mathematicians, a Swiss and an Italian. For 10 points, name this constant, symbolized by a Greek gamma.

This is the type of statistical test that uses a distribution named for a British-born statistician writing as "Student" at the Guinness brewery. It is used for small samples. For 10 points, name this test.

This is the name for the line that divides a segment into two equal parts at a right angle. Every point on it is equidistant from the two endpoints of the segment. The three of them in a triangle meet at the circumcenter. For 10 points, name this line.
This is the measure of how much a curve bends, equal to the reciprocal of the radius of the osculating circle. A straight line has zero of it. For 10 points, name this geometric quantity.

This conjecture states that every simply connected, closed three-dimensional manifold is homeomorphic to the three-sphere. It was proved by Grigori Perelman using Ricci flow, following a program of Richard Hamilton. Perelman declined the Fields Medal and the Millennium Prize for it. For 10 points, name this conjecture, the first Millennium Prize Problem to be solved.

q: A Greek scholar who was head of the Library of Alexandria and also measured the circumference of the Earth devised this method for finding primes. One lists the integers from two up, then repeatedly crosses out all multiples of each surviving number. The numbers that remain are prime. For 10 points, name this ancient algorithm named for that scholar.

This function of a real number returns its distance from zero, so the value for negative three is three. Its graph is V-shaped with a corner at the origin. It is written with two vertical bars around the input. For 10 points, name this function that makes negatives positive.

This number, approximately 1.618, equals one plus the square root of five, all divided by two. The ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers approaches it. It is denoted by a Greek letter and appears in the pentagram and in Euclid's extreme and mean ratio. For 10 points, name this ratio.

This three-dimensional shape has volume four thirds pi r cubed and surface area four pi r squared. Archimedes was so proud of relating its volume to that of a circumscribed cylinder that it was reportedly shown on his tomb. Every point on its surface is the same distance from its center. For 10 points, name this round solid.

This class of problems consists of decision problems whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time. Whether it equals the class P of problems solvable in polynomial time is one of the Millennium Prize Problems. Stephen Cook and Leonid Levin proved that the satisfiability problem is complete for it. For 10 points, name this complexity class abbreviated with two letters.

This problem asks whether a program will finish running or loop forever for a given input. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no general algorithm can decide it for all program-input pairs. The proof uses a diagonalization argument. For 10 points, name this undecidable problem.

This graph traversal algorithm extends a shortest-path method by adding a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance to the goal, ordering nodes by the sum of cost so far and that estimate. It is optimal if the heuristic never overestimates. It was developed at the Stanford Research Institute for the robot Shakey. For 10 points, name this pathfinding algorithm commonly used in video games, whose name is a letter followed by a punctuation symbol.

This sorting algorithm repeatedly divides the list in half, sorts each half recursively, and then combines them in order. It is stable and always runs in n log n time, but needs extra memory. John von Neumann described it in 1945. For 10 points, name this divide-and-conquer sort.

This is the term for a program that translates human-readable source code into machine code for execution, as opposed to an interpreter. For 10 points, name this type of program that includes GCC and Clang.

This is the term for a self-balancing binary search tree named for two Soviet mathematicians, in which the heights of the two subtrees of any node differ by at most one. For 10 points, name this tree, the first self-balancing binary search tree, with names of its inventors.

This is the 1976 public-key scheme, named for two Stanford researchers, that allows two parties to establish a shared secret over a public channel using modular exponentiation. Its security rests on the discrete logarithm problem. For 10 points, name this key exchange.

This is the architecture of most modern computers, described in 1945, where program instructions and data are stored in the same memory. It is named for a Hungarian-American mathematician. For 10 points, name this architecture.

This is the language used for most programming on Apple's iOS devices after 2014, replacing Objective-C. Its name is also a fast bird. For 10 points, name this language created by Chris Lattner at Apple.

This is the term for the principle that a database transaction is all or nothing, one of the four ACID properties. The others are consistency, isolation, and durability. For 10 points, name this property.

This 1936 mathematical model uses lambda abstraction and function application to express computation. It was developed by Alonzo Church and underlies functional programming languages like Lisp and Haskell. For 10 points, name this formal system.

This is the concept in operating systems of a small unit of execution within a process that shares memory with other such units. Using several allows a program to do tasks concurrently. For 10 points, name this unit.

This is the term for unwanted messages sent in bulk by email, usually advertising or scams. Filters use machine learning to detect it, and laws regulate it. Its name comes from a canned meat in a Monty Python sketch. For 10 points, name this nuisance in inboxes.

This protocol, created at Netscape in the 1990s and later standardized as TLS, encrypts traffic between a web browser and a server. The padlock icon in a browser indicates it. For 10 points, name this protocol abbreviated SSL.

This self-balancing tree data structure keeps data sorted and allows searches, insertions, and deletions in logarithmic time, with each node holding many keys and children. Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight invented it at Boeing in 1971. Databases and file systems use it to minimize disk reads. For 10 points, name this tree, whose name suggests letters rather than a number of branches.

This is the term for a technique where a function's results for given inputs are stored to avoid recomputation, speeding up the recursive Fibonacci algorithm. It is related to dynamic programming. For 10 points, name this technique.

This is the logic gate that outputs true only if both of its inputs are true. Its truth table has a single row with output one, when both inputs are one. In circuit diagrams it is drawn with a flat input side and a rounded output side. For 10 points, name this basic gate, often paired with OR and NOT.

This is the neural network type that uses layers of filters sliding over inputs and is widely used for image recognition. AlexNet won the ImageNet competition in 2012 using one. For 10 points, name this kind of network, abbreviated CNN.

This is the 1950 test proposed by Alan Turing in which a human judge converses with a machine and a human and tries to tell which is which. For 10 points, give the other name for the "imitation game."

This is the term for an attack in which malicious SQL code is inserted into a form field to manipulate a database query. Parameterized queries prevent it. For 10 points, name this attack, abbreviated with a three-letter language name and a word for putting something in.

This is the term for a unit of digital information equal to 1,024 bytes in some conventions, or 1,000 in SI. The next larger unit is the megabyte. For 10 points, name this unit, prefixed by a metric word for thousand.

This is the file format that is a lossy image compression standard named for the Joint Photographic Experts Group. Digital cameras commonly save photos in it. For 10 points, give this format's name, which also has a three-letter extension.

This Finnish software engineer released the first version of a free Unix-like operating system kernel in 1991 as a hobby, and later created a distributed version control system. For 10 points, name this person, whose kernel runs on Android phones and most web servers.
Answer these questions about algorithms.
parts: What kind of search checks each element of a list in order?
What technique solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing answers?
What algorithm, named for a Greek mathematician, finds the greatest common divisor of two numbers?

q: Answer these questions about programming languages.
parts: What language, developed at Mozilla and known for memory safety without a garbage collector, is named for a type of corrosion?
What language, created by John McCarthy in 1958, is known for lists written inside parentheses?
What lazy, statically typed functional language is named for the logician Curry?

q: Answer these questions about computer architecture.
parts: What component performs arithmetic and logic operations in a CPU, abbreviated ALU?
What small, fast storage locations inside the CPU hold operands during execution?
What technique overlaps the stages of instruction execution to improve throughput?

q: Answer these questions about networking.
parts: What is the unique numerical label assigned to a device on a network, such as 192.168.1.1?
What device forwards data packets between networks?
What protocol assigns IP addresses automatically to devices on a network, abbreviated DHCP?

q: Answer these questions about computer scientists.
parts: Which Microsoft co-founder wrote BASIC for the Altair?
Which British scientist invented the World Wide Web?
Which American computer scientist wrote The Art of Computer Programming?

q: Answer these questions about data structures.
parts: What is the topmost node of a tree called?
What tree-based structure keeps the smallest or largest element at the top and is used for priority queues?
What structure consists of vertices connected by edges and is used to model networks?

q: Answer these questions about artificial intelligence.
parts: What term describes computers learning from data without explicit programming?
What algorithm adjusts weights in a neural network by propagating errors backward?
What 2017 neural network architecture, introduced in the paper "Attention Is All You Need," underlies modern large language models?

q: Answer these questions about software engineering.
parts: What term describes finding and fixing errors in code?
What system, created by Linus Torvalds, tracks changes in source code?
What term describes restructuring code without changing its external behavior?

q: This networking technology was developed at Xerox PARC in the 1970s by Robert Metcalfe. It connects computers in a local area network using cables with twisted pairs or fiber, and sends data in frames. Its name comes from a discredited substance once thought to carry light waves. For 10 points, name this wired networking standard.

This design philosophy for processors uses a small set of simple instructions that each execute in about one cycle. David Patterson helped popularize it, and ARM chips are based on it. It contrasts with CISC designs like x86. For 10 points, name this approach, abbreviated by four letters.

This is the term for a synchronization primitive that ensures only one thread at a time enters a critical section of code. A thread must acquire it before accessing shared data, and releases it afterward. Its name is a contraction of "mutual exclusion." For 10 points, name this lock.

This is the smallest controllable element of a digital image, arranged in a grid on a screen. A display's resolution is given by the number of them across and down, such as 1920 by 1080. Its name contracts "picture element." For 10 points, name this unit of an image.

This lossless compression method, developed by an MIT student in 1952, assigns shorter binary codes to more frequent symbols by building a tree from the bottom up. The resulting codes are prefix-free, so no code is the start of another. It is used in file formats like ZIP and JPEG. For 10 points, name this coding scheme named for its inventor.

Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms both find this subgraph of a connected weighted graph. It touches every vertex, contains no cycles, and has the smallest possible total edge weight. It is used in designing efficient networks of cables. For 10 points, name this kind of subgraph, abbreviated MST.

This automatic memory management process, introduced for Lisp by John McCarthy, reclaims memory occupied by objects that a program can no longer reach. Java and Python both use it. Mark-and-sweep is one technique for doing it. For 10 points, name this process.

This is a network security system that monitors and filters incoming and outgoing traffic according to rules. It sits between a trusted internal network and untrusted networks like the Internet. Its name comes from a wall that stops the spread of flames in a building. For 10 points, name this system.

This criterion, proposed by Karl Popper in The Logic of Scientific Discovery, holds that a claim is scientific only if some possible observation could show it to be false. Popper used it to distinguish science from pseudoscience such as astrology and Freudian psychoanalysis. It replaced verification as a demarcation standard. For 10 points, name this principle of testable refutation.

Thomas Kuhn introduced this term in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions to describe a sudden change in the basic assumptions of a field, as in the move from Ptolemaic to Copernican astronomy. Periods of normal science are interrupted by anomalies that lead to one of these. For 10 points, name this kind of "shift."

This French chemist is called the father of modern chemistry. He showed that combustion involves combination with oxygen, named hydrogen and oxygen, and stated a law of conservation of mass. His wife Marie-Anne helped translate and illustrate his work before he was guillotined in 1794. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This Russian physiologist won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his work on digestion. He noticed that dogs began to salivate at the sound of a bell that had been paired with food, establishing a type of learning named for him. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This Swedish chemist invented dynamite in 1867 and left his fortune to establish prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace. For 10 points, name this man for whom the prizes are named.

This American marine biologist wrote Silent Spring in 1962, which documented the harmful effects of pesticides such as DDT on birds and other wildlife. Her book helped launch the environmental movement and led to the banning of DDT for agricultural use. For 10 points, name this author.

This British primatologist began studying wild chimpanzees at Gombe Stream in Tanzania in 1960 and observed them making and using tools. Her research was supported by the paleoanthropologist Louis Leakey. For 10 points, name this scientist, who founded an institute named for her.

This English physicist wrote A Brief History of Time and worked on black holes, showing that they emit radiation. He held the Lucasian Professorship at Cambridge and lived for decades with a motor neuron disease. For 10 points, name this theoretical physicist.

This English scientist discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, and a cage named for him blocks electric fields. A self-taught man who started as a bookbinder's apprentice, he worked at the Royal Institution under Humphry Davy. For 10 points, name this scientist for whom the farad is named.

This American inventor held over a thousand patents, including one for a practical incandescent light bulb in 1879. He established a research laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey, and also developed the phonograph. For 10 points, name this inventor.

This Serbian-American inventor developed the alternating-current induction motor and the Tesla coil. He worked for a time for Thomas Edison before partnering with George Westinghouse in the "war of the currents." For 10 points, name this inventor, for whom the SI unit of magnetic flux density is named.

This Spanish scientist used the Golgi stain to show that the nervous system is made of discrete cells, establishing the neuron doctrine. He shared the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Camillo Golgi. For 10 points, name this father of modern neuroscience, whose drawings of neurons are famous.

This Swiss psychologist proposed four stages of cognitive development in children: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational. He studied his own children closely. For 10 points, name this developmental psychologist.

This is the term for a beneficial effect felt by a patient who receives an inert treatment like a sugar pill, because they expect it to work. It is why medical trials include a control group that gets one. For 10 points, name this effect.

This principle of problem solving, named for a fourteenth-century English friar, states that among competing explanations the one with the fewest assumptions should be preferred. For 10 points, name this principle, often described as a tool for cutting away unnecessary hypotheses.

This is the system of measurement based on the meter, the kilogram, and the second, whose units are related by powers of ten. It was developed in France in the 1790s and is used by almost every country. For 10 points, name this system, whose name relates to a unit of length.

This Arab scholar of the eleventh century wrote the Book of Optics, argued that vision occurs when light enters the eye rather than leaving it, and emphasized experimentation. He is often called the father of the scientific method for his experimental approach. For 10 points, name this scholar of Basra and Cairo, known in Latin as Alhazen.

This international project, completed in 2003, determined the sequence of the roughly three billion base pairs of human DNA. It began in 1990 and was coordinated by the United States Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health. For 10 points, name this project.

This 1953 discovery by James Watson and Francis Crick, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, showed that DNA has a twisted-ladder shape. For 10 points, name this shape, described in a paper in Nature.

This is the way of writing very large or small numbers as a number between one and ten times a power of ten, such as 6.02 times ten to the twenty-third. It is used in chemistry and physics to avoid writing many zeros. For 10 points, name this notation.

This is the world's largest particle accelerator, a ring about 27 kilometers around underneath the border of France and Switzerland. It collides protons at CERN and was used to find the Higgs boson. For 10 points, name this machine, abbreviated LHC.

This is the process in which gases like carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere trap heat radiated from Earth. Without it, the planet would be much colder, but too much of it causes global warming. For 10 points, name this effect.

This 1987 international treaty phased out the production of chlorofluorocarbons and other substances that deplete the stratospheric ozone layer. It is often called the most successful environmental agreement. For 10 points, name this protocol named for a Canadian city.

This Austrian-Swedish physicist worked with Otto Hahn on uranium and, with her nephew Otto Frisch, first explained nuclear fission in 1938. Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Element 109 is named for her. For 10 points, name this scientist.
